facts.statement: CPCB estimates India generated 1,397,955.59 tonnes of e-waste in FY 2024-25.
facts.quote: As per the CPCB, e-waste generated in the country during the Financial Year (FY) 2023-24 and 2024-25 is given below: ... 2024-2025 | 13,97,955.59
facts.sourceTitle: PARLIAMENTARY QUESTION: Electronic Waste Management (Lok Sabha US Q3592)
facts.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

facts.statement: CPCB estimates India generated 1,254,286.55 tonnes of e-waste in FY 2023-24.
facts.sourceTitle: PARLIAMENTARY QUESTION: Electronic Waste Management (Lok Sabha US Q3592)
facts.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

facts.statement: CPCB reports that 70.71% of e-waste generated in FY 2024-25 was collected, dismantled and recycled or disposed, up from 61.94% in FY 2023-24.
facts.quote: Percentage (%) of e-waste waste collected, dismantled and recycled / disposed ... 2023-2024 | 12,54,286.55 | 61.94 ... 2024-2025 | 13,97,955.59 | 70.71
facts.sourceTitle: Parliament Question: E-waste processing management (Rajya Sabha)
facts.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

facts.statement: CPCB's method: national e-waste generation is estimated from registered producers' sales data and the average life of notified EEE.
facts.quote: The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) estimates the e-waste generation at national level based on the countrywide sales data provided by the registered producers, and average life of notified electrical and electronic equipment (EEE), as mandated under the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022.
facts.sourceTitle: Parliament Question: E-waste processing management (Rajya Sabha)
facts.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

facts.statement: As on 09.02.2025, 322 e-waste recyclers were registered with CPCB.
facts.quote: Currently there are 322 nos. of recyclers and 72 nos. of refurbishers registered with CPCB to cater the services for recycling / refurbishing of generated e-waste.
facts.sourceTitle: PARLIAMENT QUESTION: MANAGEMENT OF GROWING E-WASTE IN THE COUNTRY (Rajya Sabha US Q1006)
facts.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

facts.statement: The reported processing capacity of the 322 CPCB-registered e-waste recyclers is 2,208,918.064 MT per annum (as on 09.02.2025).
facts.quote: The reported processing capacity of 322 registered recyclers as on 09.02.2025 is 22,08,918.064 MT per annum and processing capacity of 72 registered refurbishers is 92,042.18 MT per annum.
facts.sourceTitle: PARLIAMENT QUESTION: MANAGEMENT OF GROWING E-WASTE IN THE COUNTRY (Rajya Sabha US Q1006)
facts.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

facts.statement: As on 09.02.2025, 72 refurbishers were registered with CPCB, with a processing capacity of 92,042.18 MT per annum.
facts.quote: processing capacity of 72 registered refurbishers is 92,042.18 MT per annum
facts.sourceTitle: PARLIAMENT QUESTION: MANAGEMENT OF GROWING E-WASTE IN THE COUNTRY (Rajya Sabha US Q1006)
facts.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

facts.statement: Registered e-waste recyclers are located in 19 States; Uttar Pradesh had the most (125) in FY 2024-25.
facts.quote: The registered e-waste Recyclers are presently located in 19 States. ... Uttar Pradesh | 74 | 125
facts.sourceTitle: Parliament Question: E-waste processing management (Rajya Sabha)
facts.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

facts.statement: Global E-waste Monitor 2024: India generated 4,137 million kg of e-waste in 2022 (2.9 kg per capita), and 59.6 million kg was documented as formally collected and recycled.
facts.quote: India Asia 4137 2,9 59,6 Communication with Assocham India in the context of this report: ... Yes Yes Yes No
facts.sourceTitle: The Global E-waste Monitor 2024, Annex 2. Datasets (p. 126); columns: e-waste generated (million kg), e-waste generated (kg/capita), e-waste documented as formally collected and recycled (million kg)
facts.publisher: ITU and UNITAR (Baldé, Kuehr et al.)

facts.statement: In the GEM 2024 country table, India (4,137 million kg) is the third-largest generator, after China (12,066) and the United States (7,188).
facts.quote: China Asia 12066 8,5 1951,7 ... United [States of America] Americas 7188 21,3 4052,8 ... India Asia 4137 2,9 59,6
facts.sourceTitle: The Global E-waste Monitor 2024, Annex 2. Datasets

facts.statement: The world generated a record 62 billion kg of e-waste in 2022 (7.8 kg per capita); 22.3% was documented as formally collected and recycled.
facts.quote: In 2022, the world produced 62 billion kg of e-waste (7.8 kg per capita), of which 13.8 billion kg (1.7 kg per capita) were documented as formally collected, for a global formally documented collection and recycling rate of 22.3 per cent.
facts.sourceTitle: The Global E-waste Monitor 2024, Chapter 3. Key Global Statistics (p. 28)

facts.statement: A 2011 Rajya Sabha Secretariat research report stated that the unorganised sector was handling more than 90% of India's e-waste. This is a 2011 estimate; no newer official figure was found.
facts.unit: % of e-waste handled by the unorganised sector (more than; 2011)
facts.quote: However, it is the unorganized sector which is currently handling more than 90 per cent of the e-waste generated in the country.
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste in India (Research Unit, LARRDIS), p. 107

facts.statement: In a peer-reviewed survey of 1,039 young adults aged 18-22 in New Delhi, 46.5% said they keep obsolete mobile phones stored at home, and only 3.8% take them to a recycling centre.
facts.quote: Table 8. Disposal behavior of obsolete mobile phones: I keep it stored at home 483 46.5 ... I sell it to the scrap dealers or 'kawariwalas' at certain cost 116 11.2 ... I take it to the recycling center 39 3.8 ... Total 1039 100.0
facts.sourceTitle: Understanding consumers' perspectives of electronic waste in an emerging economy: a case study of New Delhi, India (Energy, Ecology & Environment; doi:10.1007/s40974-022-00242-9)
facts.publisher: Borthakur A. and Singh P., Springer (open access via PubMed Central PMC8853223)

facts.statement: In the same New Delhi survey, 11.2% sell old phones to scrap dealers (kabadiwalas), and 20.0% give them away free to siblings or relatives.
facts.quote: I give it to someone for free (e.g., to my siblings/relatives/others) 208 20.0; I sell it to the scrap dealers or 'kawariwalas' at certain cost 116 11.2
facts.sourceTitle: Understanding consumers' perspectives of electronic waste in an emerging economy: a case study of New Delhi, India
facts.publisher: Borthakur A. and Singh P., Energy, Ecology & Environment (Springer)

facts.statement: WEEE Forum (International E-waste Day 2022): of about 16 billion mobile phones possessed worldwide, about 5.3 billion were expected to become waste in 2022.
facts.quote: Experts expect roughly 5.3 billion mobile / smartphones will drop out of use this year.
facts.sourceTitle: International E-waste Day: Of ~16 Billion Mobile Phones Possessed Worldwide, ~5.3 Billion will Become Waste in 2022

facts.statement: WEEE Forum surveys (June to September 2022) of 8,775 European households: the average household has 74 e-products, of which 13 are hoarded (9 unused but working, 4 broken). Mobile and smartphones rank 4th among hoarded small EEE.
facts.quote: The surveys show that, of 8,775 European households in six countries ... the average household contains 74 e-products ... Of that 74 average total e-products, 13 are being hoarded (9 of them unused but working, 4 broken).
facts.sourceTitle: International E-waste Day: Of ~16 Billion Mobile Phones Possessed Worldwide, ~5.3 Billion will Become Waste in 2022
facts.publisher: WEEE Forum (results consolidated by UNITAR SCYCLE)

facts.statement: WEEE Forum 2022, Europe: the top reason for hoarding WEEE is 'I might use it again in the future' (46%); 'presence of sensitive data' was cited by only 2%.
facts.quote: Top 5 reasons for hoarding WEEE of any kind, Europe: I might use it again in the future (46%) I plan on selling it / giving it away (15%) It has sentimental value (13%) It might have value in the future (9%) I don't know how to dispose of it (7%) Others ... Presence of sensitive data (2%)
facts.sourceTitle: International E-waste Day: Of ~16 Billion Mobile Phones Possessed Worldwide, ~5.3 Billion will Become Waste in 2022

facts.statement: YouGov 2024 (UK, 3,119 mobile owners): 52% still have their old handsets.
facts.quote: The most common action is keeping old phones, with 52% of Britons saying they still have their old handsets.
facts.sourceTitle: What do Britons do with their old phones? Half of them keep it (YouGov Custom Research; fieldwork 29 April - 4 May 2024)

facts.statement: YouGov 2024 (UK): of people who keep old phones, 26% worry about security and others accessing their data, and 19% don't know how to wipe their data.
facts.quote: A quarter (26%) are worried about security and don't want others to access their data. ... One in five Britons (19%) don't know how to wipe their data
facts.sourceTitle: What do Britons do with their old phones? Half of them keep it

facts.statement: The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 were notified as G.S.R. 801(E) on 2 November 2022 and came into force on 1 April 2023, superseding the 2016 Rules.
facts.quote: New Delhi, the 2nd November 2022 G.S.R. 801(E) ... (2) They shall come into force from the 1st day of April, 2023.
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, Sec. 3(i)
facts.publisher: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (copy hosted by CPCB)

facts.statement: The Rules cover 106 EEE items listed in Schedule I, including discarded mobile phones, computers and UPS systems.
facts.quote: These Rules are regulating 106 Electrical and Electronic Equipment (EEE) listed in Schedule-I of the said Rules, including discarded mobile phones, computers and UPS systems.
facts.sourceTitle: PARLIAMENTARY QUESTION: Electronic Waste Management

facts.statement: A 'bulk consumer' is any entity that used at least 1,000 units of Schedule I EEE in a financial year, including e-retailers. Bulk consumers must hand their e-waste only to a registered producer, refurbisher or recycler (Rule 8).
facts.unit: units of EEE per financial year (bulk consumer threshold)
facts.quote: 'bulk consumer' means any entity which has used at least one thousand units of electrical and electronic equipment listed in Schedule I, at any point of time in the particular Financial Year and includes e-retailer; ... 8. Responsibilities of bulk consumer. - Bulk consumers of electrical and electronic equipment listed in Schedule I shall ensure that e-waste generated by them shall be handed over only to the registered producer, refurbisher or recycler.
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, Rules 3(1)(b) and 8

facts.statement: EPR means producers must meet recycling targets only through registered recyclers. Under Schedule III, the target by weight is 60% of EEE placed on the market in year Y-X (X = average life) for 2023-24 and 2024-25, 70% for 2025-26 and 2026-27, and 80% from 2027-28.
facts.quote: 'extended producer responsibility' means responsibility of any producer of electrical or electronic equipment as given in Schedule-I for meeting recycling targets as per Schedule-III and Schedule-IV, only through registered recyclers of e-waste ... 2023-2024 60% ... 2025-2026 70% ... 2027-2028 80% of the quantity of an EEE placed in the market in year Y-X, where 'X' is the average life of that product
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, Rule 3(1)(m) and Schedule III

facts.statement: Manufacturers, producers, refurbishers and recyclers must register on the CPCB portal, and registered entities may not deal with unregistered ones (Rule 4).
facts.quote: (3) No entity referred in sub-rule (1) shall carry out any business without registration. (4) The entities registered under sub-rule (1) shall not deal with any unregistered manufacturer, producer, recycler and refurbisher.
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, Rule 4

facts.statement: Mobile phones are Schedule I code ITEW15 ('Cellular telephones'). Phablets are ITEW20.
facts.quote: Cellular telephones ITEW15 ... Phablets ITEW20
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, Schedule I (i) Information technology and telecommunication equipment

facts.statement: Laptops are Schedule I code ITEW3; notebooks are ITEW4 and notepad computers are ITEW5.
facts.quote: Personal Computing: Laptop Computers (Central Processing unit with input and output devices) ITEW3; Personal Computing: Notebook Computers ITEW4; Personal Computing: Notepad Computers ITEW5
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, Schedule I

facts.statement: Desktop personal computers are Schedule I code ITEW2.
facts.quote: Personal Computing: Personal Computers (Central Processing unit with input and output devices) ITEW2
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, Schedule I

facts.statement: Tablets are Schedule I code ITEW19.
facts.quote: Tablets, I-PAD ITEW19
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, Schedule I

facts.statement: Printers, including cartridges, are Schedule I code ITEW6; scanners are ITEW21.
facts.quote: Printers including cartridges ITEW6 ... Scanners ITEW21
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, Schedule I

facts.statement: Monitors fall under Schedule I code CEEW6 ('Screen, Electronic Photo frames, Electronic Display Panel, Monitors').
facts.quote: Screen, Electronic Photo frames, Electronic Display Panel, Monitors CEEW6
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, Schedule I (ii) Consumer Electrical and Electronics and Photovoltaic Panels

facts.statement: Television sets, including LCD and LED, are Schedule I code CEEW1.
facts.quote: Television sets (including sets based on Liquid Crystal Display and light Emitting Diode Technology) CEEW1
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, Schedule I

facts.statement: Routers are Schedule I code ITEW22 and modems are ITEW26. UPS is ITEW24 and electronic data storage devices are ITEW27.
facts.quote: Routers ITEW22 ... UPS ITEW24 ... Modems ITEW26 ... Electronic data storage devices ITEW27
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, Schedule I

facts.statement: The E-Waste Rules 2022 do not apply to waste batteries; those are covered by the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 (Rule 2(a)).
facts.quote: 2. Application. - These rules shall apply to every manufacturer, producer refurbisher, dismantler and recycler ... but shall not apply to - (a) waste batteries as covered under the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022;
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, Rule 2

facts.statement: The Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 (S.O. 3984(E), dated 22 Aug 2022, published in the Gazette on 24 Aug 2022) apply to all batteries regardless of chemistry, and to consumers.
facts.quote: New Delhi, the 22nd August, 2022 S.O. 3984(E) ... 2. Application. - (1) These rules shall apply to, -(i) Producer, dealer, consumer, entities involved in collection, segregation, transportation, re-furbishment and recycling of Waste Battery; (ii) all types of batteries regardless of chemistry, shape, volume, weight, material composition and use.
facts.sourceTitle: Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, Sec. 3(ii), No. 3810
facts.publisher: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

facts.statement: Consumers must discard waste batteries separately from other waste and give them to an entity engaged in collection, refurbishment or recycling (Rule 5).
facts.quote: 5. Functions of Consumer. - (1) It will be the responsibility of consumer, - (i) to discard Waste Battery separately from other waste streams especially from mixed waste, domestic waste streams; (ii) to ensure that Waste Battery are disposed off in an environment friendly manner by giving it to an entity engaged in collection or refurbishment or recycling;
facts.sourceTitle: Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, Rule 5

facts.statement: A 'portable battery' is a sealed battery under 5 kg that is not made for industrial, EV or automotive use. This covers phone and laptop packs.
facts.quote: 'Portable battery' means Battery that is sealed, less than five kilograms, not made for industrial purposes, electric vehicle or to be used as an Automotive Battery;
facts.sourceTitle: Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, Rule 3(1)(t)

facts.statement: The E-Waste (Management) Amendment Rules, 2024 (G.S.R. 164(E), 8 March 2024) let CPCB set a price band for EPR certificates: 100% (highest) and 30% (lowest) of the environmental compensation for non-fulfilment of EPR.
facts.unit: EPR certificate price band, as % of environmental compensation
facts.quote: (9) The Central Pollution Control Board shall fix the highest and lowest price for exchange of extended producer responsibility certificates which shall be equal to hundred per cent and thirty per cent, respectively of the environmental compensation for non-fulfilment of extended producer responsibility obligation under rule 22.
facts.sourceTitle: E-Waste (Management) Amendment Rules, 2024, G.S.R. 164(E)

facts.statement: EPA (citing USGS 2006): for every million cell phones recycled, 35,000 lb of copper, 772 lb of silver, 75 lb of gold and 33 lb of palladium can be recovered.
facts.unit: lb of gold per million phones (also 35,000 lb Cu, 772 lb Ag, 33 lb Pd)
facts.quote: For every million cell phones we recycle, 35 thousand pounds of copper, 772 pounds of silver, 75 pounds of gold and 33 pounds of palladium can be recovered.
facts.sourceTitle: Electronics Donation and Recycling

facts.statement: USGS Fact Sheet 2006-3097: a typical 113 g cell phone (excluding battery and charger) contains 16 g copper, 0.35 g silver, 0.034 g gold, 0.015 g palladium and 0.00034 g platinum.
facts.unit: g gold per phone (113 g phone, excl. battery and charger)
facts.quote: Table 1 ... Metal content ... estimated for a typical cell phone ... Copper 16 ... Silver 0.35 ... Gold 0.034 ... Palladiun 0.015 ... Platinum 0.00034 [Wt (g)]; The average weight (wt) of a cell phone is estimated to be 113 grams (g), exclusive of batteries and charger (Nokia, 2005).
facts.sourceTitle: Recycled Cell Phones - A Treasure Trove of Valuable Metals (Fact Sheet 2006-3097), Table 1

facts.statement: EPA: recycling one million laptops saves energy equivalent to the electricity used by more than 3,500 U.S. homes in a year. EPA introduces this under 'In 2006, U.S. Geological Survey estimated', but the figure does not appear in the USGS fact sheet EPA links to.
facts.unit: U.S. homes' annual electricity per million laptops recycled (more than)
facts.quote: Recycling one million laptops saves the energy equivalent to the electricity used by more than 3,500 U.S. homes in a year.
facts.sourceTitle: Electronics Donation and Recycling

facts.statement: EPA: Li-ion batteries in the trash or curbside recycling can be damaged or crushed in transport or sorting, creating a fire hazard.
facts.quote: Additionally, if the battery or electronic device that contains the battery is disposed of in the trash or placed in the municipal recycling bin with household recyclables such as plastic, paper or glass, it may become damaged or crushed in transport or from processing and sorting equipment, creating a fire hazard.
facts.sourceTitle: Used Lithium-Ion Batteries

facts.statement: EPA handling advice: bag each battery or device separately, tape the terminals, and note that even used batteries can hold enough energy to start fires.
facts.quote: Handling precautions: Place each battery or device containing a battery in a separate plastic bag. Place non-conductive tape (e.g., electrical tape) over the battery's terminals. ... Even used batteries can have enough energy to injure or start fires.
facts.sourceTitle: Used Lithium-Ion Batteries

facts.statement: WHO: unsound e-waste recycling can release up to 1,000 different chemical substances, including neurotoxicants such as lead. Children and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable.
facts.quote: When e-waste is recycling using unsound activities, it can release up to 1000 different chemical substances into the environment, including known neurotoxicants such as lead (3). Pregnant women and children are particularly vulnerable due to their pathways of exposure and developmental status.
facts.sourceTitle: Electronic waste (e-waste) - Fact sheet

facts.statement: WHO: open burning and heating are the most hazardous informal e-waste activities. Linked health effects include stillbirth and premature birth, neurodevelopmental effects from lead, and reduced lung function and asthma.
facts.quote: Open burning and heating are considered the most hazardous activities due to the toxic fumes created. ... adverse neonatal outcomes, including increased rates of stillbirth and premature birth; neurodevelopment, learning and behaviour outcomes, especially associated with lead released through informal e-waste recycling activities; reduced lung and respiratory function and increased asthma incidence
facts.sourceTitle: Electronic waste (e-waste) - Fact sheet

facts.statement: WHO: the ILO estimated that as many as 16.5 million children were working in the industrial sector in 2020, of which waste processing is a subsector.
facts.unit: million children in the industrial sector (2020)
facts.quote: The International Labour Organization (ILO) estimates that 16.5 million children were working in the industrial sector in 2020
facts.sourceTitle: Electronic waste (e-waste) - Fact sheet
